newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Britomart float promoted to brokers - NZ Herald.
newsitem.headline: Britomart float promoted to brokers - NZ Herald.

text.p: Britomart developer Pacific Capital Assets began promoting its NZ$100 million float among New Zealand brokers at private functions, The New Zealand Herald reported on Thursday.
However, the nature of the promotion raises questions on the application of the Securities Act.

Certain people are exempt from the provisions of the Act preventing pre-prospectus publicity, but Securities Commission executive director John Farrell said that "the question of a breach may arise if brokers are selling to their clients".
"It would certainly be a breach of the law to obtain any commitment from any individual person or member of the public before the prospectus was registered."
Pacific Capital, on the advice of its lead manager, County NatWest, has maintained a silence about any details of the float, claiming this would amount to advertising.

This is despite a Securities Act section which stipulates details which can be stated before the issue of a prospectus, and despite some details being revealed last week by an Australian director, David Sutton.
Managing director Jihong Lu said Sutton had not been authorised to make his statements.
The float was promoted through Asia, particularly Malaysia, in May with astounding success. Even then, the promoters expected the eventual float would be oversubscribed.
The promotion that began in New Zealand on Wednesday was for brokers and analysts, with brokers seeking commitments from clients to take an allocation.
Given the overseas support already, those allocations are likely to be scaled down.
Lu said the public issue was due to open next Wednesday, and allocations would be decided the day before.
That will leave the general public investor out in the cold, although Pacific Capital has said it wants public support for its infrastructure investments.

This week's promotions have not been with a copy of the prospectus but through a slide show carrying the disclaimer that the contents were prepared "to assist prospective sub-underwriters in making a decision whether or not to become a sub-underwriter"
The Companies Office record on Pacific Capital shows that 1000 shares were taken up by Jihong Lu, his wife and a company executive on incorporation, the Herald reports.
In addition, major shareholders Hudson Corporate, Savoy Trust (Lu's family trust), Idris Hydraulic of Malaysia, and First KL took up 70 million shares on May 19.
Another 35 million second-ranking redeemable shares were created at the same time.
These are understood to be the second half of the public package, coming in behind the 65 million $1 contributory shares revealed by Sutton.
The contributory shares would be 50c payable on subscription and the balance in three years.
These are details which could have been revealed to the public under section 3(6) of the Securities Act, which allows a limited pre-prospectus statement.

Brokers have sought support for the issue from clients. The question, in terms of the Act, is whether they can all be classified as being among the categories not excluded from pre-prospectus information, such as habitual investors.
Lu said the presentations were to brokers, but agreed it was "fair comment" that they were seeking to fill allocations among their clients.
